strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: agent count affects both exploration and coordination, so a curriculum that always progresses from fewer to more agents can be inappropriate. Allowing adaptive movement toward a specified target count is well motivated.

Combining self-paced distribution updates with critic-loss-based task selection is a simple, potentially useful contribution. The SPRLM comparison usefully isolates the objective substitution within the same curriculum framework.

The experiments provide promising evidence of practical effectiveness. SPMARL improves mean evaluation performance during training on Simple-Spread and substantially outperforms SPRLM on the harder Protoss tasks. The appendix broadens evaluation with Terran, Zerg, and dense-reward BenchMARL environments.

Reporting target performance alongside training returns and generated curricula makes the results informative. Confidence intervals, significance tests, threshold sensitivity experiments, implementation notes, hyperparameter tables, and a source-code link strengthen the empirical presentation.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as learning progress is not established. Sections 2 and 5 assert that value loss inherently measures policy change and that converged value estimates imply little further policy updating. Accurate evaluation of the current policy does not imply policy optimality or a vanishing actor gradient. Moreover, squared prediction error can remain large because of irreducible reward or transition noise, even when policy improvement is impossible. The method may be a useful heuristic, but its principal explanation needs either appropriately qualified claims or direct evidence connecting the score to subsequent policy improvement.

The variance analysis does not substantiate the claimed reduction in estimation variance. Appendix A.3.4 computes dispersion across approximately 25 different contexts, which mixes task heterogeneity with sampling error. It also compares episode returns against squared, temporally averaged prediction errors under different training processes. These quantities have different scales, and their numerical ordering can change under reward rescaling. Repeated measurements under matched policies and contexts, with appropriate normalization and attention to temporal correlation, are needed to support this central argument.

The comparisons leave important alternative explanations unresolved. Simple-Spread uses an increasing Linear curriculum despite the paper establishing that additional agents ease reward discovery; a decreasing schedule is an essential control. A uniform context sampler followed by target-task training would also test how much adaptation contributes beyond task mixing. Furthermore, ALPGMM and VACL lack the target-convergence mechanism emphasized by SPMARL. Their weaker target performance therefore does not establish that SPMARL alleviates credit assignment. The paper provides no direct credit-assignment diagnostic or controlled experiment separating that explanation from differences in target exposure.

The originality discussion omits closely related task-prioritization work, particularly Prioritized Level Replay, which already uses value-error-related signals to prioritize environments. The analogy to prioritized experience replay is insufficient to distinguish the proposed learning-progress objective from existing environment-level prioritization. The combination with self-paced optimization and variable agent counts could still constitute a contribution, but its relationship to this prior work needs clearer treatment.

Several presentation details limit interpretation and reproduction. Equation 4 defines the target as a discounted return, whereas Appendix A.3.4 describes a one-step bootstrapped target; the precise implemented score, normalization, and timing relative to critic updates should be explicit. Claims of consistently surpassing all baselines also exceed the reported evidence: Table 2 finds no significant advantage over SPRLM on XOR or ALPGMM on Protoss 5v5 and 6v6. Overall, the practical results have substantive merit, but the unsupported mechanism claims and missing experimental controls make weak rejection more appropriate at present.
